LESSON 14 OF 106·Networking Fundamentals

LANs, Wi-Fi and Wireless Frame Security

How a LAN delivers a frame to one device, what Wi-Fi encryption protects inside a wireless frame, and what anyone in radio range can still observe.

Beginner2 min
Why this matters

A wired local network is a shared medium that the switch largely isolates, while Wi-Fi is a shared radio that anyone nearby can hear and join. That difference is the whole security problem with wireless.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • check the security mode in use, and treat WEP and WPA as unacceptable rather than as weak
  • verify the network uses WPA3 or at least WPA2 with AES
  • look for extra access points you did not install
  • treat the passphrase as a shared secret, so anyone who knows it can decrypt traffic for everyone

How it works

  • Ethernet switches learn which port a device is on and forward frames accordingly, which isolates traffic between ports.
  • A hub or an unmanaged switch forwards everything to every port, so any device on it can see traffic not addressed to it.
  • Wireless frames are radio broadcasts, so every nearby device with the same key can read the traffic by default.
  • WPA2 introduced the four-way handshake, which authenticates the access point and derives keys, but the older WPA handshake allowed an offline dictionary attack.
  • WPA3 replaces that handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, which resists offline guessing and encrypts even open networks.

The background

  • WEP used a short key and a weak cipher and was broken within years of being standard, which is why it is now prohibited.
  • WPA was a stopgap that fixed a serious flaw but left the offline attack available against a captured handshake.
  • WPA2 fixed the handshake, but many implementations shipped with weak default keys or poor password handling.
  • WPA3 addresses both, and enterprises are also moving to per-user credentials with certificate-based admission.

Real-world examples

  • An open Wi-Fi network with no encryption lets anyone nearby read and modify traffic that was expected to be private.
  • A captured WPA2 handshake can be attacked offline, so a strong passphrase matters far more than the standard you chose.
  • A rogue access point advertising a familiar name can intercept traffic even when the real network is correctly secured.

What to look for

  • Check the security mode in use, and treat WEP and WPA as unacceptable rather than as weak.
  • Verify the network uses WPA3 or at least WPA2 with AES.
  • Look for extra access points you did not install.
  • Treat the passphrase as a shared secret, so anyone who knows it can decrypt traffic for everyone.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use WPA3 where clients support it, and WPA2-AES otherwise.
  • Use a long passphrase, and change it if it is ever exposed.
  • Keep a known network of authorised devices and alert on additions.
  • Segment wireless clients from internal systems so a compromised device gains less.
